Disruptive Behavior in a Child

oppositional defiant disorder · conduct disorder · intermittent explosive disorder · disruptive mood dysregulation disorder · the antisocial personality age ruleDefiance, violated rights, impulsive rage, or constant irritability between outbursts?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sort by what the child does and the mood between episodes:

  • Oppositional defiant disorder: angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behavior, or vindictiveness; 4 or more symptoms for 6 months, with someone other than a sibling
  • Conduct disorder: 3 or more in 12 months, from any of aggression to people or animals, property destruction, deceit or theft, or serious rule violations such as truancy
  • Intermittent explosive disorder: outbursts out of proportion and not premeditated, verbal aggression on average twice a week for 3 months, or 3 outbursts destroying property in 12 months; age 6 or older
  • Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder: severe outbursts 3 or more times a week, irritable or angry mood most of the day nearly every day between them, in 2 or more settings, for 12 months or more without a 3-month gap; first diagnosed from 6 to 18, onset before 10

Antisocial personality disorder needs age 18 or older and conduct disorder before 15.

Tantrums in a preschooler who cannot make himself understood point to a language disorder.

Diagnosis
Defining rules Frequency in oppositional defiant disorder – under age 5, most days; age 5 or older, at least once a week · Precedence – when disruptive mood dysregulation disorder is met, do not also diagnose oppositional defiant or intermittent explosive disorder · ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) – disruptive and impulsive, but without aggression or a pattern of violating norms · Substance use – the sole diagnosis when the behavior occurs only with use
Disruptive behavior: the differential
DisorderBehaviorBetween episodesAge rule
Oppositional defiant disorderArgues, defies, vindictive; no stealing or violation of others' rightsAngry or irritable mood counts as a symptomFrequency depends on age 5
Conduct disorderAggression, destruction, theft, truancyPersistent pattern; lies for gain or to avoid consequencesOnset before 10 carries a poorer prognosis
Intermittent explosive disorderImpulsive outbursts out of proportionAppropriate behavior; no deceit, theft or truancyAge 6 or older
Disruptive mood dysregulation disorderSevere outbursts, 3 or more a weekIrritable or angry most of the day, nearly every dayDiagnosed 6 to 18; onset before 10
Antisocial personality disorderPervasive disregard for others' rights–18 or older, conduct disorder before 15
Management and treatment
By diagnosis Oppositional defiant disorder – parent management training first; medication is sometimes considered when aggression cannot be managed with psychosocial care alone · Conduct disorder – parent management training; cognitive behavioral therapy for older children; multisystemic therapy for severe adolescent cases; a second-generation antipsychotic (eg, risperidone) only for severe aggression unresponsive to these; treat comorbid ADHD or substance use alongside · Intermittent explosive disorder – no FDA (Food and Drug Administration) approved treatment; parent management training and cognitive behavioral therapy with parent management are commonly used; drugs for persistent aggression are unproven
Practice
  1. 15-year-old boy brought in after a second police warning a year of skipping school, stealing from stores and forging his father's checks set fire to a neighbor's shed last month T 36.8 °C · urine toxicology negative → Conduct disorder → theft, forgery, truancy and fire setting over a year violate others' rights and major rules: conduct disorder; oppositional defiant disorder is less severe and lacks theft and destruction, and antisocial personality disorder needs age 18 or older
  2. 8-year-old girl, 9 months of arguing with her parents and teacher refuses requests, blames her sister, says spiteful things every week no fights, theft, damage, lying, truancy or running away T 36.9 °C · examination normal → Oppositional defiant disorder → argumentative, defiant and vindictive behavior toward adults for at least 6 months, weekly or more: oppositional defiant disorder; conduct disorder is more severe, and she shows none of its categories; there are no severe outbursts with irritability between them
  3. 16-year-old boy, since age 14 erupts over small frustrations broke things in 3 separate outbursts this year; ashamed afterward even-tempered between outbursts; no lying, theft or truancy HR 78/min · urine toxicology negative → Intermittent explosive disorder → impulsive outbursts out of proportion and not premeditated, with calm between them: intermittent explosive disorder; conduct disorder adds deceit, theft or truancy, and disruptive mood dysregulation disorder needs persistent irritability between outbursts and onset before age 10
  4. 10-year-old boy, 14 months of rages at home and at school screams and throws things 4 or 5 times weekly over small limits angry or grumpy most of every day between began at age 8 T 37.0 °C · examination normal → Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder → severe outbursts 3 or more times a week with irritable mood between them for over 12 months, starting before age 10: disruptive mood dysregulation disorder; when its criteria are met, oppositional defiant disorder and intermittent explosive disorder are not diagnosed
  5. 9-year-old boy, a year of fights, theft and truancy attentive in class; no substance use no aggression since a school change; parents ask what helps T 36.8 °C · BP 104/66 mm Hg → Parent management training → conduct disorder is treated mainly with psychosocial care: behavioral parent management training, with cognitive behavioral therapy for older children; multisystemic therapy is for adolescents with more severe symptoms, and risperidone is reserved for severe aggression unresponsive to psychosocial care
  6. 5-year-old boy whose kindergarten teacher reports he shoves classmates who misunderstand him speaks in short, jumbled sentences; cannot count to 10 or name letters buttons his coat, hops on one foot, follows game rules hearing normal · T 36.7 °C → Language disorder → at 5, children speak in full sentences, count to 10 and name letters; aggression from not being understood points to a language disorder when other milestones are on target, and neither disruptive mood dysregulation disorder nor intermittent explosive disorder is diagnosed before age 6
Pairs with School Difficulty in a Child: inattention and learning, not norm-breaking. Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth: is language delayed for age?
Transferable rule

Name the behavior first, then check the age gate: no antisocial personality disorder before 18, and no disruptive mood dysregulation disorder before 6.
